nature-eco-045.title: Edge effects: life on the border of a fragment
nature-eco-045.text: About 70% of the world's remaining forest lies within one kilometer of a forest edge. Edges are different places. Light, temperature and wind there differ from the interior and favor different species. These changed conditions are called edge effects, and {{ref:nature-nbs-115}} creates them. Fires become more likely at edges as humidity drops and temperature and wind rise. Exotic and pest species establish easily in disturbed edges. Small fragments are poor homes for species that need interior habitat.

nature-eco-039.title: Only 4 percent of the world's mammals are wild
nature-eco-039.text: Of all mammal biomass on Earth today, only 4% is wild mammals. Livestock makes up 60% and humans 36%. That split is the result of a long fall in the total mass of wild mammals over the past 50,000 years, while humans and livestock multiplied. Wild land mammals are believed to weigh seven times less in total than in prehistoric times. The total mass of marine mammals has fallen fivefold.

nature-eco-040.title: Freshwater life: the fastest decline of all
nature-eco-040.text: Rivers, lakes, swamps and deltas cover just 1% of Earth's surface, yet they are home to about one third of vertebrate species. Their species are vanishing especially fast, at twice the rate of land or ocean species. Populations of migratory freshwater fish have fallen by 76% since 1970. About one in three freshwater fish species is threatened with extinction.

nature-eco-038.title: Too many people or too much consumption?
nature-eco-038.text: Is the deeper cause of biodiversity loss the number of people, or how much they consume? Many scientists, and the assessment described in {{ref:nature-eco-123}}, name growing human numbers and excessive consumption as the main underlying drivers. Critics point elsewhere. They say habitat loss comes mainly from growth in export commodities such as soybean and oil palm, much of it for livestock feed or biofuel in richer economies. Country data add a twist. A country's GDP correlates strongly with its environmental footprint, while its population size correlates negatively with footprint per person. Scholars still disagree on which driver matters most.

nature-eco-034.title: Are all invaders villains? Critics of the invasive label
nature-eco-034.text: Not every newcomer is a villain, some scientists argue. They say not all biological invasions are harmful and that the language of invasion misleads. They describe an "effective invasion", in which an alien species fills a vacant niche and joins local food webs without displacing natives. Some urge that species moving to escape a warming climate be treated as refugees rather than invaders. Entomologist Chris D. Thomas goes further, arguing that most introduced species are neutral or beneficial. His remains a minority view against the consensus, described in {{ref:nature-eco-026}}, that invaders are mainly harmful.

nature-eco-033.title: Gene drives: rigging inheritance to remove invaders
nature-eco-033.text: Normally, offspring have a 50:50 chance of inheriting either version of a gene. A gene drive tilts those odds. It is a genetic-engineering technique that makes a chosen gene spread through a population faster than normal inheritance allows, by suppressing the unwanted version. It has been proposed as a way to wipe out invasive animals, such as the invasive mammals of New Zealand.

nature-eco-028.title: Invasion pathways: how species hitch rides around the world
nature-eco-028.text: About 100 cane toads brought to Australia have become over 200 million. They were brought in on purpose to fight pests, and the plan backfired. Invasion pathways are the routes, mostly human, by which non-native species reach new places. People carry organisms faster and farther than natural range expansion, both on purpose and by accident. Repeated traffic, such as ships between ports, creates recurring chances for arrival and establishment, called high propagule pressure. A 2008 study found shipping, through fouled hulls and ballast water, to be the dominant pathway for marine invaders.

nature-eco-029.title: Biosecurity: stopping pests at the border
nature-eco-029.text: Borders are a first line of defense against pests. Biosecurity quarantine means inspection and quarantine rules on traded goods and ships that aim to stop pests and invasive species from crossing borders. The first global standards were agreed in 1994, including the WTO's Sanitary and Phytosanitary Agreement. They aimed to block agricultural pests while still allowing farm exports. At sea, the International Maritime Organization oversees the Ballast Water Management Convention. The agreement described in {{ref:nature-gov-015}} is the most significant international agreement on invasive species, but most of its measures are voluntary and unspecific.

nature-eco-032.title: Weed risk assessment: screening plants before they arrive
nature-eco-032.text: Most plant introductions are intentional, so there is a chance to stop a harmful one before it happens. Weed risk assessment is a standardized questionnaire that scores how likely a plant is to cause harm in a new environment, before it is introduced. The total score is tied to a management action, such as "prevent introduction".

nature-eco-122.title: Genetic erosion: losing the variety within species
nature-eco-122.text: Keeping at least 90% of the northern quoll's genetic diversity requires conserving at least eight populations across Australia. Genetic erosion is any decrease in genetic diversity, whether natural or caused by people. Each organism's genome, its full set of genes, is unique. When one dies without breeding, any unique genes it carried are lost. Habitat loss and fragmentation, often from farming and infrastructure, speed the process, and so does diversity that is already low. Small populations are most at risk. Low diversity brings inbreeding and weak immunity, which can 'fast-track' a species toward extinction. In crops, the main driver is replacing local varieties of plants and animals with non-local ones, often commercial varieties. Many researchers see modern agriculture's push toward genetic and ecological uniformity as the main problem in managing farm ecosystems. Science offers some safeguards, but many are still too expensive. Protecting habitat and letting species live naturally in it remains the best defense.

nature-eco-072.title: Agricultural biodiversity: the living variety behind food
nature-eco-072.text: By a conservative estimate, about 6,000 species are commonly used for food. Agricultural biodiversity is the part of biodiversity that matters for farming. It is the variety of plants, animals and microbes, at gene, species and ecosystem levels, that sustains food and farm production. Farmers, herders, fishers and forest dwellers manage it. It gives rural livelihoods stability, adaptability and resilience, and it is critical for adapting to and slowing climate change. It also earns income, through food and raw materials and through services such as pollinating crops, controlling pests and cycling nutrients. Of the 115 major crop species grown worldwide, 75% rely on pollinators. Urbanization, deforestation, single-crop farming, abandoned traditional practices and Westernized diets all threaten it. Its loss leads to genetic erosion, including the loss of landraces and breeds adapted to their local area.

nature-eco-074.title: Ex situ conservation: seed banks and frozen backups
nature-eco-074.text: Over 7 million samples are held in 1,750 genebanks worldwide. Ex situ conservation keeps species or genetic material away from their natural habitat, in places such as seed banks, genebanks, botanical gardens and cryobanks, which store material frozen. It is considered a fairly reliable way to keep genetic diversity over the long term, because stored material changes little. That stillness is also a limit. In situ conservation, described in {{ref:nature-eco-131}}, lets species keep evolving in response to natural and human pressures. Practitioners recommend combining both.

nature-eco-042.title: The hidden price of converting a habitat
nature-eco-042.text: Turning forest into row crops can raise a country's food supply. Yet the same land may be worth more left natural, supplying clean water, timber, tourism based on nature, or flood and drought control. What people give up when a habitat is destroyed is the value the land would have produced if left alone. That forgone value is the opportunity cost of habitat conversion.

nature-eco-043.title: Direct and deeper causes of forest loss
nature-eco-043.text: In 2002, Geist and Lambin reviewed 152 case studies of forest loss in the tropics. They separated the direct activities that clear forest, the proximate causes, from the deeper demographic, economic and political forces behind them. The proximate causes clustered as agricultural expansion (96%), infrastructure expansion (72%) and wood extraction (67%). Extending roads and transport was the largest single proximate factor. Small farmers clearing new plots in rotation, described in {{ref:nature-res-155}}, were not the main cause in every region. Most cases combined three to four underlying causes driving two to three proximate ones. So no single universal policy can control tropical deforestation.

nature-eco-055.title: Cattle, crops and roads: what drives deforestation
nature-eco-055.text: Around 80% of converted land in the Amazon is used to rear cattle, making beef the primary driver there. Drivers of deforestation are the activities and forces that lead people to clear forests: chiefly farming and ranching, but also logging, mining, roads and wider economic pressures. Agricultural expansion remains the main driver of forest loss, fragmentation and loss of forest biodiversity. One breakdown attributes 48% of deforestation to subsistence farming, 32% to commercial agriculture, 14% to logging and 5% to fuel wood. By the 1990s, though, most clearing came from industrial factors such as extractive industries, large-scale ranching and extensive agriculture. Since 2001, commodity-driven clearing, which is more likely to be permanent, has made up about a quarter of all damage to forests. Roads open the way: about 90% of deforestation in most of the Amazon has occurred within 100 km of one. The role of human numbers is contested. One study found high fertility a primary driver in only 8% of tropical cases, and sources disagree on its weight against commodity demand.

nature-eco-100.title: Captive breeding: zoos as a last refuge
nature-eco-100.text: Some of the oldest examples of captive breeding come from the animal collections of European and Asian rulers, which kept species such as Père David's deer. Captive breeding means breeding rare or endangered species in controlled settings such as zoos and reserves, to keep them from going extinct. It suits some animals better than others. Highly mobile species, such as migratory cranes and fishes, are hard to breed this way. Numbers matter too. Too small a captive population risks inbreeding from a reduced gene pool.

nature-eco-101.title: Can owning rhinos save them? Private ownership and wildlife
nature-eco-101.text: Southern black and white rhinoceros populations have grown substantially through legal, for-profit private farming. The idea is that letting people legally own and profit from endangered animals gives them reasons to protect rather than poach them, an application of {{ref:nature-econ-621}}. Wildlife tourism and sales give rhino owners strong economic incentives to look after the animals. The approach can backfire. Turtle farmers, for instance, may seek out the last wild specimens as breeding stock.

nature-eco-102.title: Redefining recovery: panthers, cougars and realistic goals
nature-eco-102.text: Florida panthers were saved by bringing in Texas cougars, creating well-adapted panther–cougar hybrids. Shifting recovery baselines means redefining what counts as recovery for a species near extinction, to set more realistic goals. Options include moving a species to better habitat, letting it breed with similar species, or accepting a smaller stable population. It is a last resort. It carries extra risks and is usually tried only after recovery within the natural range has failed.

nature-eco-106.title: Coextinction: when one loss takes another with it
nature-eco-106.text: When a species dies out, it can take others with it. Coextinction is the loss of one species because another species it depends on has gone extinct. Parasitic insects can die out after their hosts are lost. Predators can vanish when their prey disappears, and a plant can vanish when its pollinator does. Coextinction is especially common when a keystone species, one with an outsized effect on its ecosystem, goes extinct.

nature-eco-109.title: De-extinction: cloning the mammoth and the dodo
nature-eco-109.text: The Pyrenean ibex has been cloned before, and it joins the mammoth, the thylacine and the dodo on the list of proposed targets. De-extinction is the proposal to bring an extinct species back to life by cloning it from DNA in its remains. Success would need enough clones from different individuals to form a viable population. It seems possible in theory. IUCN guidelines from 2016 hold that an extinct species cannot be perfectly recreated, so the results are called 'proxy species'. Supporters say it could restore lost ecological functions. Critics call it 'playing God' and fear disease, hybridization and animal suffering.

nature-eco-107.title: Genetic pollution: extinction by interbreeding
nature-eco-107.text: The greatest threat to the endangered wild water buffalo is interbreeding with the abundant domestic water buffalo. That is genetic pollution: uncontrolled interbreeding with introduced or hybrid populations that swamps a native species' gene pool. It most threatens rare species that meet abundant ones, whose hybrids deplete the pure gene pool. Such extinctions may be invisible, because they need not show in an animal's outward appearance.

nature-eco-108.title: Lazarus taxa: species that return from the dead
nature-eco-108.text: In 1938 a living coelacanth was found off South Africa. The fish had been known only from fossils and thought extinct since the end of the Cretaceous. A Lazarus taxon is a species or group thought to be extinct that is later found again. Such reappearances show how hard it is to establish exactly when a species has gone extinct, a difficulty {{ref:nature-eco-105}} also notes.

nature-eco-089.title: The insect decline: fewer bugs, uncertain numbers
nature-eco-089.text: In German nature reserves, the seasonal biomass of flying insects fell by 76% over 1989–2016. Insects account for up to 90% of all animal species, so their fate matters. Since the 2010s, researchers have reported a widespread fall in insect numbers across many groups, sometimes reaching extinction. Estimates of insect species at risk of extinction range from 10% to 40%. A 2020 meta-analysis, which pooled 166 long-term studies, found land insects declining about 9% per decade, while freshwater insects rose 11% per decade. One study ranked the causes: habitat loss to cities and to farms that push land hard, pesticide and fertilizer pollution, pathogens and introduced species, then climate change. The decline threatens insect-eating birds and mammals, and services such as pollinating crops and disposing of waste. Global trends are hard to judge. Data vary by time, place and species and come mostly from Western Europe and North America. A 2019 review projected that 40% of insect species could go extinct within decades, but that claim was challenged, and global estimates remain uncertain.

nature-eco-065.title: Sea otters, urchins and kelp: cascades of overharvest
nature-eco-065.text: When hunters removed sea otters, the sea urchins they kept in check multiplied. The urchins stripped kelp beds into barren ground, causing secondary extinctions. This is a cascade effect of overexploitation: overharvesting removes a key species, especially a top predator, and the effects ripple through the food web. Without the predator, its prey multiply and overexploit their own food, sometimes until they too collapse. Recovery is possible. After a 1911 treaty protected the last 32 sea otters in one group, they multiplied and the depleted areas slowly recovered.

nature-eco-064.title: Fish stock collapse: the cod that never came back
nature-eco-064.text: Atlantic cod collapsed abruptly in 1992 after heavy exploitation and failed to recover even after fishing stopped. A fish stock collapse is the crash of a fished population, conventionally when its biomass falls by more than 95 percent from the highest level recorded. Pushing harvests past the largest catch that can be sustained, explained in {{ref:nature-res-013}}, leads to collapse. That limit usually sits near 30% of pre-harvest biomass, and about 25% of the world's fish populations are already below it. A 2008 study found strong evidence that individual transferable quotas, tradable shares of an allowed catch, help prevent collapses and restore declining fisheries.

nature-eco-025.title: Amphibians and the fungus that is wiping them out
nature-eco-025.text: Amphibians survived three earlier mass extinctions over more than 300 million years. Today they are the most endangered vertebrate group. Frog and salamander populations are crashing worldwide, driven partly by chytridiomycosis, a fungal disease spread by human travel and the wildlife trade. The disease has caused severe declines in over 500 amphibian species and perhaps 90 extinctions. Amphibian decline is treated as an indicator of environmental degradation, part of the wider wave described in {{ref:nature-eco-022}}.

nature-eco-024.title: Did hunters kill the mammoths? The megafauna debate
nature-eco-024.text: Between 52,000 and 9,000 BC, 178 species of the world's largest mammals died out. What killed these megafauna? Their disappearance correlates with the arrival of humans, and human activity has been the main cause of mammal extinctions since the Late Pleistocene. A rival theory holds that climate change near the end of the Pleistocene, the last ice age, stressed them to extinction. Some scientists think hunting and climate acted together, and sources still disagree on the balance. Africa lost the fewest megafauna, possibly because its animals evolved alongside humans and learned to fear them.

nature-eco-023.title: Is a sixth mass extinction already here?
nature-eco-023.text: A mass extinction is defined as the loss of at least 75% of species within a geologically short period, less than 2 million years. By that yardstick, are today's losses already one? Some researchers call recent losses dramatic and serious, but not yet a mass extinction like the five great ones described in {{ref:nature-eco-113}}. Others, including a 2022 review in Biological Reviews, argue that a sixth mass extinction caused by human activity is already under way. Estimates of species lost per year range widely, from 1.5 to 40,000. All of them point to human activity as the cause.
